So TensorRT utilizes the tensorCores in the chip and along with Cuda cores, and to be able to do that we need to convert the Pytorch model(.pth file) to tensorRT model(.engine file). I exported the oytorch model to an ONNX file first then used trtexec to convert them in the Jetson Orin nano itself. I have tried various Quantization (FP32, FP16, INT8 and also Pytorch(FP16). The sweet spot for me which I realized through running all of them would be the TensorRT FP16 model which balances out the accuracy, performance and efficiency really well, and still gives headroom for various other tasks. Mind it that this is still in pure python and ROS2 running on CPU. If we utilize IsaacROS on Cpp we could get this to even more efficiency.

Alan Lockett that is a fair technical point. In a strict  benchmark, we should indeed compare at ISO-precision.
However the context here was an Engineering Case Study for a student comparing the typical Research State (Standard PyTorch/FP32 model) directly against the Deployment State (TensorRT/FP16 model/engine) We wanted to quantify the total efficiency gain a student like my self gets by moving from their training laptop to a fully optimized edge pipeline.
But you are right that the precision drop accounts for a large chunk of that gain. So I plan to actually running a follow-up benchmark comparing PyTorch AMP (FP16) vs TensorRT (FP16) and many other too at the same time to isolate the gains specifically. Will share those results soon enough.
Dr. Jonas Kölzer Actually when I ran the model, I could see the difference in accuracy. It was the basic model. But yup.

Ryan Hanzlick Yeah so to clarify, both benchmarks in this post are running on the exact same NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano. The Gain is purely from the software stack (PyTorch Runtime vs. TensorRT Runtime). And yup we are comparing the standard training precision (PyTorch FP32) against the optimized deployment target (TensorRT FP16) and in terms of accuracy we saw negligible degradation like really negligible switching to FP16 for this specific lane detection task and in terms of speed, the smaller parameterization and kernel fusion is exactly what gives the 4x efficiency gain shown here.

Jürgen Fey Yes, Its really moving fast. You are right that 4 high-res streams might choke the Orin Nano bandwidth(it sure will), but for our specific use case this optimization is comfortable for us.
The fact that we can now run VSLAM(Which I actually did) and Perception on a 15/25W board that fits in the palm of a hand would have been a dream just 3 or 4 years ago. Exciting times to be building.

Martijn Handels Thats a good perspective. You are right 4-6 cameras changes the math entirely, and the memory bandwidth becomes the bottleneck even more then the computation. Thats exactly why we obsess over this optimization step.
If a single camera model consumes 85% GPU (PyTorch) a multi-camera setup is impossible. By optimizing it down to 20% we actually make a multi-camera pipeline mathematically feasible at least on this specific hardware. We are not building custom chips like Tesla yet, but for the our constraints, squeezing every thing out of the Orin Nano is our best path forward from my perspective.

Ardy Seto Priambodo Actually it goes beyond just FP16 quantization. When we compile to a TensorRT Engine the builder perform several graph level optimization too like layer fusion, kernel auto tuning and dynamic tensor memory etc etc.

Suraj Waghmare 
We utilize Deep Learning (UFLD) rather than Canny/Sobel filters, as it is far more robust to lighting changes and texture-less roads.
For scenarios with missing markings, we implement a multi-stage fallback logic: if the model confidence drops, the system projects a Ghost Path which is a straight trajectory and alerts the safety driver, ensuring the vehicle doesnt behave out of control and also we can implement emergeny conditions too.
Also as UFLD is great there are other models which too does perform better than UFLD as those can handle horizontal turns much better and this project was mainly focused on optimizing a model using tensor cores to run more efficiently but keeping the same perfomance.
